AAVM: A fund of other ETFs that together apply value and momentum factor investing to smaller companies around the world. It is a systematic, research-driven holding from Alpha Architect that hunts for the long-run factor premiums in global small and mid caps rather than picking individual stocks.
ACSP: Exposure to an index that recreates autocallable notes on the big US stock index: structured payoffs that produce income while markets cooperate. It packages a strategy usually sold as bank notes into a tradable fund, with the same quirk that sharp market falls can turn income into losses.
BITS: Two crypto exposures in one actively managed fund: shares of blockchain companies plus long positions in bitcoin futures traded in the US. It aims to capture the crypto economy from both the business and the coin side, and both parts are volatile, so swings are large.
BREE: Emerging market stocks picked with MFS's blended research process, combining analyst work with quantitative models, and heavily weighted to Asian technology at about 46 percent. It is a growth-leaning developing markets holding that accepts chip and internet concentration in exchange for those markets' biggest success stories.
BRSM: Small and midsize US companies selected with MFS's blended research, mixing analyst judgment with quantitative models across industry, technology, finance and health care. It is a diversified mid-market growth and value holding, positioned between volatile small caps and the steadier large company funds.
BTA: A tactical basket of alternative investments held through other ETFs: currencies, commodities, gold and futures-based strategies among them. It is a diversifier built to behave differently from stocks and bonds, shifting its mix as conditions change, and it can sit in cash-like holdings when signals are poor.
CBTJ: Bitcoin exposure wrapped in a structured protection design: Treasury bills and options aim to guard most of the downside, the 80 in its name, over the year starting each January. In exchange, bitcoin's gains are capped, so it suits investors who want some crypto exposure without the full plunge risk.
CCSB: Short-term bonds carrying green or sustainability labels, meaning the money funds projects like clean energy or efficient buildings, with average maturity under five years. It is a cautious income holding for investors who want their bond money aimed at environmental projects without long-term rate risk.
CPSO: Options on a fund of the largest US companies structured to protect against losses over the year starting each October, in exchange for a cap on gains. It is Calamos's defined protection design, meant for investors who want stock market exposure with the downside for the year largely removed.
CRDT: A go-anywhere income portfolio spanning US and foreign bonds and other income securities, using leverage and derivatives to hunt for yield opportunistically. That flexible, amplified design can pay more than cautious bond funds, but it also magnifies losses and makes the fund harder to predict.
DEEP: The smallest and cheapest US companies: a deep value index of small and micro-cap stocks trading at low prices relative to their fundamentals. It is an aggressive bet that the market's most ignored leftovers will recover, and such tiny stocks can sit still or slide for long stretches.
DIVY: Around thirty dividend-paying US companies, mostly midsize, spread across banks, health care, consumer firms and energy. It is an income holding built on stock picking rather than an index, favoring steady payers, and its mid-cap lean makes it somewhat steadier than small-cap dividend funds.
EYEG: Investment grade bonds issued by companies, actively managed by AllianceBernstein across industries and maturities. It is a core corporate bond holding for interest income, with managers adjusting credit quality and maturity mix as conditions change rather than simply copying the corporate bond index.
EZRO: A defensive sector rotation system holding other US ETFs, shifting among stock sectors according to its AlphaDroid model's signals. It currently leans heavily on technology, but the point is the rotation: the model aims to favor stronger sectors and turn cautious when its measures of risk rise.
GOOP: A single-stock income strategy on Alphabet, the parent of Google: options on its shares generate payments while keeping some exposure to the stock's movement. Everything rides on one technology giant, so income is the goal and gains are limited by the options sold against the position.
HBMX: A concentrated stack of memory chip companies, the makers of DRAM and flash storage, with derivatives adding to the exposure. Memory prices move in violent cycles, so this is an amplified bet on one of the most boom-and-bust corners of the technology industry.
HFMF: Futures contracts across stocks, bonds, currencies and commodities, traded by trend and other systematic strategies to imitate the returns of hedge fund managed futures programs. It is a diversifier designed to zig when stocks zag, especially in long market slides, though it can drift in flat markets.
HYBX: Actively managed high yield bonds chosen by TCW managers across lower-rated corporate debt. It is an income holding built on manager research into which junk borrowers look sound, so it aims to dodge the weakest credits that a plain high yield index holds by default.
IIGD: US investment grade bonds with the highest quality scores in their universe, emphasizing strong borrowers and defensive traits, in shorter maturities. It is a cautious income holding designed for capital preservation first, accepting lower yields than funds willing to own shakier corporate credit.
INYY: A single-stock income strategy built on Intel shares, using options on that one chipmaker to generate regular payments. Because everything rides on one company plus the options overlay, it is highly concentrated: income can be generous, but gains are capped and the chipmaker's drops hit directly.
IVSS: A focused set of small and midsize US companies, as few as fifteen or so, chosen by Applied Finance for intrinsic value: what the business is truly worth versus its price. It is a concentrated value holding where thorough appraisal of each company drives results.
JIDE: Actively managed stocks from developed markets abroad, with banks the largest slice, chosen under a dynamic process that adjusts country and style tilts. It fills the international slot with manager judgment rather than an index, leaning on Europe and Japan style markets and their currencies.
JLVP: Large US value stocks with a twist: alongside the shares it owns, the fund takes short positions betting against selected companies. That long-short overlay aims to add return and soften market drops, making it a more hedged value holding than a plain index of cheap big stocks.
LCOW: Big US companies with a rare cash record: at least ten straight years of positive free cash flow, plus high cash margins and returns on capital. It is a quality-focused core holding that screens for proven cash generators rather than size or cheapness, and technology cash machines feature heavily.
LFEQ: Large US stocks when a trend model says be invested, and cash-like safety when it says step aside: the Ned Davis model behind it flips between long and flat. It is a defensive core holding for investors who want the market's gains with an automatic exit in downtrends.
MCVT: Convertible bonds from companies with strong growth traits: debt that pays interest but can convert into stock if the company prospers. It is a hybrid holding that aims to join much of a growth stock's upside with a bond's floor under it, managed for total return.
METW: A single-stock trading fund aiming to deliver about 120 percent of Meta Platforms' return each calendar week, using swaps and shares, while paying weekly distributions. It resets its leverage weekly and rides entirely on one social media giant, so it suits short-term trades, not holding.
MFSD: Short-term debt from governments, companies and securitized loans, managed by MFS for income with limited sensitivity to interest rate moves. It sits between a money market fund and a full bond fund: steadier than longer bonds, with a bit more yield and a bit more price movement.
MYCK: Corporate bonds that mature in 2031, part of a series of target-year bond funds, so the holdings roll down toward cash as 2031 approaches. It works like a ladder rung for a known future expense, paying company bond interest with less and less rate sensitivity as the end nears.
NOVM: Options referencing a fund of the largest US companies aim for the maximum available buffer against losses over a one-year outcome period starting each November. In exchange for that deeper protection, the cap on gains is lower than on lighter buffer funds, so it is the cautious end of the range.
NVYY: An income strategy built on derivatives referencing a fund of Nvidia shares, designed to convert that one chip giant's big price swings into regular payments. It is highly concentrated by design: the income aim is generous, but Nvidia's sharp drops pass through and gains are limited by the strategy.
PCPP: A ready-made balanced portfolio following a published model index: a bit over half in global stocks, plus bonds, cash and other assets. One fund covers several asset classes at a moderate risk level, with financial stocks the biggest single theme inside the equity side.
PQJL: Options tied to the Nasdaq-100 create a buffer that absorbs a set slice of losses over a twelve-month outcome period starting each July, in exchange for a cap on gains. Because the underlying stocks lean heavily on technology, it pairs that protection with more growth and more swing than broad market buffers.
PQOC: Options tied to the Nasdaq-100 create a buffer that absorbs a set slice of losses over a twelve-month outcome period starting each October, in exchange for a cap on gains. Because the underlying stocks lean heavily on technology, it pairs that protection with more growth and more swing than broad market buffers.
PRVS: A concentrated portfolio of large US companies bought at value prices, run by Parnassus, a firm known for responsible investing. With fewer holdings than most value funds, each pick matters more, and the approach favors established companies its managers judge temporarily out of favor.
PSCF: Small US financial companies: community and regional banks make up about two thirds, with small real estate trusts most of the rest. It is a focused bet on local American finance, so it depends on small-town lending health and property markets rather than Wall Street giants.
QBSV: Options tied to the S&P 500, structured to absorb the first 5 percent of losses over each outcome period in exchange for a cap on gains. It is the slimmest buffer in the AllianzIM range, a light cushion for investors who want some protection while giving up as little upside as possible.
QDTY: A synthetic covered call strategy on the Nasdaq-100 using options that expire the same day they are bought, designed to pay income weekly. The tech-heavy index means bigger swings than a broad market version, and the same-day calls give up most gains on strong rally days.
QNXT: The Nasdaq-100 with its thirty biggest members removed, leaving roughly seventy smaller companies from that index across technology, consumer, health care and industry. It is a growth holding for investors who already own the giants elsewhere and want the index's next tier to get its own room to run.
REIX: Real estate and infrastructure companies worldwide: property trusts at about half, plus utilities, industrial operators and energy infrastructure. It is an income-leaning holding on the world's buildings, toll roads, pipelines and data centers, and it tends to react strongly to interest rate moves.
ROMO: US stocks selected by a robust momentum system from Newfound and ReSolve that favors strong, steady price trends and builds in risk controls. It is a core style equity holding with a defensive streak, designed to cut exposure when momentum breaks down rather than ride every fall to the bottom.
SGRW: Small US growth companies picked by Granahan managers, concentrated in technology and health care innovators. It is an aggressive growth holding: small companies with fast-growing sales can multiply in value, and they also fall hardest when investors turn away from risk and growth stories.
TGLB: Large companies across global developed markets, actively picked, with technology about a third and the rest spread across finance, media, industry and health care. It is a core worldwide stock holding run on manager research, including US giants alongside their European and Japanese peers.
TLTP: Long-term US Treasury bonds paired with weekly at-the-money call options sold against them to harvest premium income. Bond funds usually pay modest interest, so this design aims for a much higher income stream from the options, while the long Treasury holdings still swing hard when rates move.
WISE: Companies building generative artificial intelligence: chip designers, cloud platforms, software firms and the data infrastructure behind AI models. It is a focused bet on the generative AI wave specifically, so it is more concentrated than broad AI or technology funds and swings with that theme's hype cycle.
WMSB: A multisector bond portfolio run by Weitz managers, free to roam across government, corporate, mortgage and other debt in search of value. It is a flexible core income holding from a value-minded shop, so its mix can look quite different from the standard bond index at any time.
WTIP: A model-driven inflation defense built mainly from inflation-protected Treasury bonds, with room for other inflation-sensitive assets alongside. It aims to hold its value when prices rise and inflation bites, serving as the protective corner of a portfolio rather than a growth engine.
XLVI: Health care stocks, the full sector from drugmakers to insurers, paired with an options program that collects premium income on top. It aims for sector returns plus extra income with a slightly smoother ride, giving up some upside when health care shares climb quickly.
XNOV: Options on a fund of the largest US companies shape an enhanced return over the year from November: gains get a boost up to a cap, with a moderate buffer against losses. It sits between plain buffer and growth funds, trading some protection for a faster start on the upside.
YQQQ: An income strategy built to move against the Nasdaq-100: options give indirect inverse exposure to that tech-heavy index while generating regular payments. It is a bearish, tactical trade rather than an investment, with gains from index falls limited by design and losses if the rally continues.
